The System of the Verb in Standard Biblical Prose
E.J. Revell
University of Toronto
This article surveys the system of the verb in the Former Prophets starting from the premises (advanced by others) that there are two indicative “tenses”, each represented by a “simple” and a “consecutive” form in complementary distribution, and one modal system, represented by the imperative, jussive and cohortative forms, also in complementary distribution. The main thesis is that the indicative and modal systems are fully independent because (1) imperfect forms with modal value are distinguished from indicatives by their position in the clause, (2) a perfect form with waw “consecutive” following a modal has a value different from that of a modal in the same position. The article begins with a survey of the indicative system intended to set this thesis in its proper context by showing that (1) the value of any verb form depends heavily on its syntactic/semantic context, (2) despite the distinct values of the “tenses”, in many contexts either may be used to represent the same occurrence — the choice is determined by the viewpoint of the author, or by the particular implications he intends to convey. The article concludes with a survey of the way this system developed to the end of the Biblical period.
1.1 The basic system of the verb in standard biblical prose is best described as using a set of indicative forms representing two categories — here called QTL and YQTL — and a set of modal forms representing one category. The various verb forms are used in this system as follows:
Indicative Affirmative Negative
QTL
Within clause perfect לא + perfect
Clause initial waw consec. imperf. לא + perfect
YQTL
Within clause imperfect לא + imperfect
Clause initial waw consec. perfect לא + imperfect
MODAL
1st person cohortative אל + cohortative¹
2nd person imperative אל + jussive
3rd person jussive אל + jussive
(1) The negative אל is followed by a cohortative form in 2 Sam. 24:14; Jer. 17:18, 18, 18:18; Jonah 1:14; Ps 25:2, 31:2, 18, 69:15, 71:1. The form is not cohortative in 2 Sam.
1
Variations in the basic pattern of usage are described below.
1.2 This description is not new, either for the indicative system or for the modal.However, the treatment of the two as parts of a single system appears to raise a problem which is generally overlooked. If the imperfect and the waw consecutive perfect are conditioned variants representing a single category, then either (a) the waw consecutive perfect cannot act as a variant of modal forms, or (b) if the waw consecutive perfect can act as a variant of the modals, then this must be true for the imperfect as well. The formal distinction between modal and imperfect forms is generally accompanied by a semantic difference. It would be unreasonable to deny that the semantic fields of modal and YQTL overlap, so that the forms which represent them may appear as free variants. If the description in #1.1 is correct, however, it ought to be possible to specify with some precision the contexts in which either modal or indicative can occur.
1.3 This paper follows Joüon (see n. 3) in arguing that the first alternative is correct. The waw consecutive perfect does not act as a variant of modal forms, even though in some contexts either this form or a modal might be used. A survey of the use of indicative forms preceding the discussion of this point shows that the use of verb forms in biblical prose is often not rigidly determined. In many situations the speaker/narrator may choose either a QTL or a YQTL form according
13:25 (תדלוף); Ps. 25:20 (אבוש); Job 32:21 (אשא, see n. 17); and 1 Chron. 21:13 (אפל = 2 Sam. 24:14 אפלה). In Gen. 21:16 and Num. 11:15, the verb is from a root IIIh, and so "neutral" (see #13).
(2) For the indicative, see Blau, 1970, for the modal system, see Bergsträsser, 1929, #10a. It may be correct to regard the modal imperfect forms preserved in the text as "vestiges" in terms of morphology, as Schneider, 1985, #51.4.1 "restbestände," but this is not true in terms of syntax, as described below.
(3) Joüon (1947), p. 329, suggests that a waw consecutive perfect may be used instead of a modal simply for the sake of variety, but he considers such use "abusive," and argues "Mais de ce que, dans certains cas, on pourrait avoir aussi bien un volitif qu'un weqatalití, on ne peut pas conclure que le weqatalití ait, en soi, le sens du volitif". He continues with a discussion of this problem (#119 i-m). The standard view is given, e.g., in Gesenius-Kautzsch, 1910, #112 p-r, Blau, 1976, #60.1. Some scholars have recently argued that imperfect and jussive forms do not differ significantly in meaning — as in Johnson, 1979, P. 97, Zuber, 1986, 143-146 — but have not treated the imperatives in relation to this situation.
(4) The opportunity for this research was provided by a fellowship at the Institute for Advanced Studies in the Humanities at the University of Edinburgh. I am most grateful to the Director and staff of the Institute for the excellent facilities provided, and to my colleagues in the Old Testament Department at New College for helpful discussions and the use of their library.

to the particular implications it is intended to convey. It is argued here that the use of a YQTL form where a modal could be used arises from a similar choice between possible alternatives carrying different implications. The corpus on which this study is based is the material in the books of Judges, Samuel, and Kings (excluding the poetic material in: Judg. 5:2-30; 1 Sam. 2:1-10; 2 Sam. 1:19-27, 22:1-51; 2 Kgs. 19:21-28), since the value of verb forms in this straightforward historical narrative is generally clear. The purpose of this paper is the clear identification of what is standard in the usage of this corpus. The corpus undoubtedly contains material from diverse sources, but the question of whether such non-standard usage as occurs might reflect archaic or dialectal usage characteristic of particular sources cannot be dealt with here.
THE USE OF INDICATIVES
2.1 The meaning carried by the opposition of the two categories of the indicative, QTL and YQTL, has been much debated. It seems to me that it is most easily presented as one of time reference: QTL 'past' versus YQTL 'present/future'. While the ease of such presentation is no doubt partly due to the fact that English uses a tense system, there is no real reason to suppose that Hebrew does not.
(a) The fact that forms typically representing past time may represent future, and vice versa, under particular conditions, does not show that the basic system is not one of tense (pace Driver, 1892, #1). The same phenomenon occurs in English, as in the examples in Lyons (1986), p. 239.
(b) The criterion by which the value of a form must be judged is not its historical origin, but its use within the corpus. No matter what the origin of the waw consecutive verb forms, those which occur in the corpus must be regarded as syntactically conditioned variants of the perfect and imperfect forms. This removes any obstacle to considering the categories they represent as tense categories, as argued in Blau, 1970.
(c) The Hebrew of post-biblical times certainly used a tense system, and the same is widely assumed for the ancestor of the biblical language, as vestigially represented by the 'preterite' (or waw consecutive) use of the imperfect form. It seems likely, a priori, that the system of the intervening period would also have been one of tense. The QTL:YQTL
(5) A verbless clause is also often a possibility. These clauses are not systematically considered here, but note the use of such clauses in: 1 Kgs. 6:27 (quoted in #3.1); 2 Sam. 5:19 (#4.2); 2 Sam. 23:14 (#11.1).
4 E. J. REVELL [4]
opposition is easily interpreted as one of tense in almost all cases. It is consequently here treated as such, even though it could be interpreted in other ways.
2.2 It is important to note that the time reference of the two categories in relation to the speaker/narrator is not absolute, but is conditioned by the time reference of the context in which the verb form is used. This, like the categories themselves, can be categorized as ‘past’ or ‘present/future’.The value, in terms of English, of YQTL forms differs markedly in these two temporal contexts. The difference in value of QTL forms is much less noticeable.
THE USE OF INDICATIVE FORMS: QTL
3.1 QTL forms characteristically present an event which has occurred in the past from the point of view of the speaker or narrator, as in
Judg. 1:7 כאשר עשיתי כן שלם לי אלהים ‘As I have done, so God has repaid me.’ As this example shows, a QTL form may represent a single event, as שלם, or events which were repeated, habitual, or continuous over a period, as עשיתי (as noted in Blau, 1976, #59). Such durative reference is sometimes made explicit by an adverbial, as in
2 Sam. 16:23 ועצת אחיתפל אשר יעץ בימים ההם ‘The advice of Ahitophel which he used to give (perfect) in those days,’ or by a parallel clause, as in
1 Kgs. 6:27 ... ותגע כנף האחד בקיר וכנף הכרוב השני נגעת ‘The wing of one cherub touched (waw consecutive imperfect) the wall, while the wing of the other cherub touched (participle) the other wall.’
3.2 The time reference of a QTL form may be past with reference to a present context, as that of the speaker in the example from Judg. 1:7, or that of the narrator in the example from 1 Kgs. 6:27. It may equally be past with reference to a past context, as is common in subordinate clauses in narrative, as
Judg. 1:20 ויתנו לכלב את חברון כאשר דבר משה ‘They gave Hebron to Caleb, as Moses (had) said.’
3.3 A QTL form may also represent the past relative to a future context, also usually in subordinate clauses, as The conditioning factor is often seen in terms of ‘mode of language’: narrative or discursive, as in Talstra, 1982. The validity of such a view depends on the definition of the terms. Quoted speech is ‘discursive’ when it refers to the present or future, but when referring to the past it has the characteristics of narrative, as in Jephtha’s speech in Judg. 11:15–22. It seems simpler to name the time reference of the context as the conditioning factor.
[5] THE SYSTEM OF THE VERB 5
1 Kgs. 8:47 והשיבו אל לבם בארץ אשר נשבו שם ‘They will bring (it) to mind in the land to which they (will) have been carried.’
2 Kgs. 4:24 אל תעצר לי לרכב כי אם אמרתי לך ‘Do not cease driving unless I (shall) have told you.’
3.4 As the translations show, English can use verbal phrases which accurately reflect these different temporal relationships. Where the context is future, however, a simple present form ‘unless I tell you,’ ‘the land to which they are carried’ would be more usual, and a simple past form ‘I did’ would be adequate in most cases where the context is present or past. The difference between the usages possible in English is basically social. The use of more or less precise forms would carry information about the educational background of the speaker, or the social context of the speech. Similar differences are possible in Hebrew. An action which is past in relation to a future event may be represented by a QTL form, as in the examples noted above. It may also be represented by a YQTL form, as
Judg. 6:26 והעלית עולה בעצי האשרה אשר תכרת ‘You will send up an offering with the wood of the Asherah which you will (have) cut down.’
It is at least reasonable to suggest that the verb form is chosen to reflect one of the possible views of the temporal relationship of the event. A YQTL form shows that it is perceived in relation to the speaker, and so as future; a QTL form shows that it is perceived in relation to its context, and so as past. The choice of forms could no doubt be similarly justified if the QTL:YQTL contrast were explained in terms of ‘complete:incomplete,’ or ‘punctual:durative’ action. What is significant for this paper is the fact that the choice of verb forms does not depend wholly on the time or nature of the action. Where the action can be understood as belonging to either of the contrasting categories, either form can be used, according to the impression of the time or of the nature of the action that the speaker wishes to convey.
4.1 In a present/future context, a QTL form may be used to represent an event which was initiated in the speaker’s past, but continues in the present. This is usual with verbs representing a condition, quality or state, where English would use a present form, as in Judg. 16:15 אהבתיך ‘I love you,’ Judg. 18:23 נזעקת ‘(What is your problem that) you are mustered?,’ and with special cases like היה ‘be,’ ידע ‘know’ and יכל ‘be able.’
4.2 This category also includes the so-called ‘Perfect of Certainty.’ A QTL form may be used to present an event which has not occurred

[6]
at the time of speaking, but which is known, or believed, to have been initiated by a decision made in the past, as in
Judg. 1:2 יהודה יעלה הנה נתתי את הארץ בידו ‘Judah will attack. I will (!) deliver the land to him.’
Judg. 7:14 נתן האלהים בידו את מדין ‘God will (!) deliver Midian to him.’
Judg. 18:10 כי נתנה אלהים בידכם ‘God will (!) deliver it to you.’
2 Sam. 9:9 כל אשר היה לשאול ... נתתי לבן אדניך I shall (!) give all that belonged to Saul to your master’s son.’
1 Kgs. 3:12 הנה נתתי לך לב חכם ‘I (hereby) give you a wise heart.’
QTL forms used in this way are sometimes called ‘performatives’: i.e. “utterances which themselves describe the speech act which they perform” (Leech, 1981, p. 322). Talstra (1982, col. 28), adapting Leech’s definition of the English usage to Hebrew, argues that the ‘perfect tense’ is characteristic of the equivalent usage in Hebrew. The resulting definition of the Hebrew performative is perfectly acceptable, but (like that of Leech for English) is very narrow. The case in 1 Kgs. 3:12 (which is translated as a performative) is the only one in the above set of examples which clearly fits it. In Judg. 1:2, the pronoun in בידו might well be regarded as the indirect object of נתתי. If this is the case, this example must be excluded along with the others. Yet the basis for the use of the perfect form would appear to be the same in all the examples. Consequently, there seems no reason to accept the claim in Talstra, 1982, col. 27, that “performative speech in Hebrew should not be explained as an aspect of any ‘basic function’ of the perfect tense.” The performative use of QTL forms is simply a subclass of the category described in this section, just as performative usage is a subclass of the use of the simple present form in English.
4.3 The use of a QTL form in these examples to represent an event which has not yet taken place is justified because a decision has been made by the speaker, whether God (Judg. 1:2, 1 Kgs. 3:12), or a human (2 Sam. 9:9), or because the speaker believes that God has made a decision because he has obtained information in a dream (Judg. 7:14), or on a tour of observation (Judg. 18:10). Such events may also be represented by YQTL forms, even where a decision has clearly been made, because the event itself is future relative to the speaker, as in
2 Sam. 5:19 עלה כי נתן אתן את הפלשתים בידך ‘Attack, because I will certainly deliver the Philistines to you.’
Judg. 1:12 אשר יכה את קרית ספר ... ונתתי לו את עכסה בתי ‘I will give my daughter to the man who attacks and captures Kiriat Sepher.’ A verbless clause, with the predicate headed by a participle, may also be used, as in

1 Sam. 23:4 כי אני נתן את פלשתים בידך ‘I (am about to) deliver the Philistines to you.’ Again, the choice of a verbless or verbal clause, or of a QTL or a YQTL form in the latter, must reflect the perceptions of the speaker, or the implications which he wishes to convey.
5 In hypothetical situations in quoted speech, a QTL form is occasionally used to represent an action which has not (yet) occurred, apparently to indicate that the action in question is unlikely or undesirable (see Driver, 1892, #19.2. although he does not connect this with his discussion of the conditionals in #138.i), as in
2 Sam. 15:33 אם עברת אתי והית עלי למשא ‘If you were to go over with me, you would be a burden to me.’ This contrasts with the use of YQTL forms standard in future conditions, as in the following sentence, where the preferred action is indicated
2 Sam. 15:34 ואם העיר תשוב ... והפרתה לי ‘But if you return to the city ... you can frustrate the counsel of Ahitophel for me.’ Similarly, in 2 Kgs. 7:4, the perfect forms in אם אמרנו ... ואם ישבנו (if we were to say ... if we were to remain ...’) clearly present courses of action undesirable to the speaker. His preference is made clear by the use of the modals in לכו ונפלה ... ‘Let us go and drop into the Syrian camp.’ The remaining examples in the corpus are: Judg. 16:17 אם גלחתי ‘If I were to be shaved’ (an eventuality that Samson neither expects nor wishes) and the interrogative החדלתי in Judg. 9:9, 11, 13 ‘Am I to give up?’, where the speakers neither expect nor wish to abandon their customary occupations. As with the other uses noted, this use of the QTL form is optional. Judah uses it in his emotive appeal to his father in
Gen. 43:9 אם לא הביאתי ... ‘If I don’t bring (perfect) him (Benjamin) back ...,’ but not in the quite different spirit in which he describes the scene to Joseph in
Gen. 44:32 אם לא אביאנו ... ‘If I don’t bring (imperfect) him ...’ Here again the choice of a QTL or a YQTL form depends on the way the speaker perceives, or wishes to present, the situation.⁷
6. A perfect form also represents QTL, and typically has past value,
(7) The use of the perfect for hypothetical actions which could occur, but have not, appears always to have this value in speech quoted in narratives, but this is not the case in the legal material presented as quoted speech in the Pentateuch, as in Num. 30:11 ואם בית אישה נדרה ‘If she has vowed in her husband’s house ...’ In this context, the perfect seems to be a free variant of the imperfect (cf. Num. 30:4 ואשה כי תדר, 30:7 ואם היו תהיה ... ‘When a woman vows ...’ and ‘If she indeed marries a man when under the vow ...’), although it might be possible to make a case for the use of the perfect as a text structuring device, to introduce subdivisions of the law on one subject. Cf. the note on this usage in Qimron, 1986, #400.19*.
8

[8]
when in clause-initial position with no conjunction prefixed. It may also have this value, in a past context, where the conjunction is prefixed. Where this occurs, the verb represents an action which accompanies, or forms a facet of, an action by the same subject represented by a preceding verb (see Driver, 1892, p. 159), as in
Judg. 3:23 ויסגר דלתות העליה בעדו ונעל ‘He closed the doors of the penthouse behind him, locking (them).’ Cf. 2 Sam. 13:18.
1 Kgs. 20:27 ובני ישראל התפקדו וכלכלו וילכו ... ‘The Israelites were mustered with provisions, and went to meet them.’ An infinitive absolute following a finite verb carries much the same meaning as the perfect in this usage,It is suggested in Huesman, 1956, that perfect forms of this sort may have originated as infinitive absolutes, but, since the phenomenon is not restricted to 3m.s forms, this cannot be true for the forms in the text as it stands. See Revell, 1985, #4. as in
2 Sam. 3:16 וילך ... הלוך ובכה אחריה ‘He went along after her weeping’ (infinitive). Compare
2 Sam. 13:19 ותלך הלוך וזעקה
‘She went along screaming’ (perfect). A waw consecutive imperfect may be used in the same situation, as in
1 Sam. 19:23 וילך הלוך ויתנבא ‘He went along, and he prophesied.’ It cannot be demonstrated from examples in this particular context that where the waw consecutive imperfect is used, the action was perceived as distinct, whereas where the perfect with conjunctive waw is used, the action was perceived as a facet of that of the preceding verb. However, this use of the perfect is distinguished from the waw consecutive use by its past context (as well as by the stress pattern in 1.s and 2.ms forms), and from the waw consecutive imperfect by its form, so it is quite reasonable to suggest that it has a distinct meaning. It shows a QTL verb to represent an action contemporary with a preceding one, contrasting with the waw consecutive imperfect which presents the two acts as in sequence.
7. Some uses of perfect or waw consecutive imperfect forms do not fit the above categories.
7.1 Perfect forms with prefixed conjunction represent past acts in some other cases.
(a) והיה introduces a section of past narrative in place of the expected ויהי ‘and it happened’ in: 1 Sam. 10:9, 13:22, 17:48, 25:20; 2 Sam. 6:16; 2 Kgs. 3:15. In 2 Sam. 16:5, ובא ‘and he came’ evidently represents a similar anomaly, since if the form were a participle heading its predicate, the subject should precede it.

THE SYSTEM OF THE VERB
9
(b) Elsewhere, in a past context, where the verb has a subject different from that of the preceding verb: Judg. 16:18; 1 Sam. 2:16, 17:35, 20:16; 2 Sam. 19:19; 1 Kgs. 18:10; 2 Kgs. 6:10, 8:10, 14:10, 22:17. Also, where the verb (despite the prefixed conjunction) is preceded by a constituent of the clause: 1 Sam. 17:20; 2 Sam. 7:11, 20:12. In addition, where the subject is the same as that of the preceding verb, in 1 Kgs. 11:10, 13:3.
7.2 A perfect form with no preceding conjunction is used where an imperfect or modal form is expected in: 1 Sam. 9:6 הלכנו; 1 Sam. 27:10 אל פשטתם; 2 Sam. 3:18 הושיע; 2 Kgs. 19:23 עליתי.
7.3 In 2 Sam. 19:2 the waw consecutive imperfect form ויתאבל ‘and he mourned’ appears to be in sequence with the preceding participle בכה in quoted speech. It could, in fact, begin the following narrative. (19:2) ‘Joab was told “The King is weeping” — and he (the king) mourned . . . (19:3) so that victory was turned to mourning for all . . . — (19:6) and Joab came to the King . . .’
More or less plausible attempts could similarly be made to show that some of the cases listed above are examples of standard usage. Other scholars might well regard as anomalies some cases that I accept as representing standard usage. In any listing, however, the anomalies would form only an insignificant proportion of the total uses of perfect and waw consecutive imperfect forms which are used consistently in the categories described in ##3-6. The point should also be made that, while some of these anomalies are not easily understood as the result of scribal error affecting the form of the verb, most of them are. This applies particularly to the use of a clause-initial perfect form with prefixed conjunction where a waw consecutive imperfect is expected. Such usage was typical of some forms of the language from early times (see Mayer [1959], Loretz [1961]) so that its occasional intrusion into standard biblical prose is not surprising.
THE USE OF INDICATIVE FORMS: YQTL
8. In terms of tense, YQTL forms refer to the present or future. Thus, in quoted speech, in a present context,
Judg. 1:1–2 מי יעלה ... יהודה יעלה ‘Who will go up? ... Judah will go up.’ Where the context is past, a YQTL form may represent an event which is present or future relative to the past context, as
Judg. 17:8 וילך האיש... לגור באשר ימצא ‘The man went to live where he could find a place.’ The English translation represents the different time reference of the two verbs by the use of the modal ‘could’ for the
10 E. J. REVELL [10]
second, but it sees both actions from the viewpoint of the speaker, as past. The Hebrew represents the second action from the viewpoint of the first. If the first action were future, the second Hebrew verb would not change in form, because the relationship of the two actions to each other would still be the same. However, the English translation must change to ‘He will go to live where he will/can find a place’ to indicate the different temporal relationship of the second action to the speaker.
9. YQTL forms, like QTL, are used both for single actions, as in the examples in Judg. 1:1-2, and for actions which are repeated, habitual, or constant. Thus, in a present or future context,
Judg. 13:14 כל אשר יצא מגפן היין ‘Everything which comes from the grape vine.’
2 Kgs. 9:20 כי בשגעון ינהג ‘He drives furiously.’ Other examples occur in Judg. 16:15; 1 Sam. 5:5, 21:12; 2 Sam. 11:20, 17:12; 2 Kgs. 18:32; and elsewhere. In a past context, such verbs present actions as repeated or habitual in the past, as in
Judg. 2:18-19 וכי הקים יהוה להם שפטים והיה יהוה עם השפט והושיעם ... כי ינחם The verbs of an English translation must indicate the fact that the events are past in relation to the speaker. ‘When the Lord had raised up a judge for them, he used to support the judge, and to rescue them, because he was moved by their pleas.’ If the introductory clause provided a present or future context, the following YQTL forms would be translated in English as present or future: ‘When the Lord raises ... he supports ...’ or ‘When the Lord will raise ... he will support ...’ In Hebrew, the future context would be indicated by the change of the initial verb to יקים, but the other verbs would not change, since the YQTL forms used for these verbs reflect the relation of the actions they represent to the context marked by the introductory verb, and this relationship does not change. Other examples occur in Judg. 6:4, 10:4, 11:40, 12:5, 14:10, etc. Where the context is past, QTL forms can be used instead of YQTL to represent these habitual actions (see #4, and cf. e.g. Judg. 2:18-19 with Judg. 3:6). As in the categories described in #4, #5, and #6, the form used is presumably chosen according to the particular implications which the speaker or narrator wishes to convey.
10. In a small group of cases, an imperfect form is used to present an event which has already occurred, as
2 Kgs. 20:14 מה אמרו האנשים האלה ומאין יבאו אליך ‘What did these men say, and where do they come from.’ Also Jos. 9:8 ויאמרו, 1 Sam. 8:7 תבואו; 1 Sam. 21:15 תבואו, תראו; 2 Sam. 1:3 תבוא. QTL forms could equally well
[11] THE SYSTEM OF THE VERB 11
have been used, as: 2 Kgs. 20:14 אמרו and נמלטתי; באו in the replies in Josh. 9:9 and 2 Sam. 1:3, corresponding to the imperfects in the preceding questions. Such actions may be seen as part of the present context ‘Where do you come from?’ or as already past ‘Where have you come from?’ Consequently, in Hebrew, they may be represented either by YQTL forms or by QTL forms.
11.1 The use of YQTL forms after אז ‘then’ also appears to be explicable in terms of the relation of the action represented to the preceding context. Where that context is future, the verb forms following אז are used as would be expected from the above description: YQTL for future action and QTL for relative past, as in
2 Sam. 5:24 יהי כשמעך את קול ... אז תחרץ כי אז יצא יהוה ‘When you hear the sound of marching ... then you will attend (imperfect), for then the Lord will have gone out (perfect) before you.’ Where the context is past, אז is usually followed by a QTL form, again consistent with the above description, as in
Judg. 8:2-3 אז רפתה רוחם ... ויאמר אליהם מה עשיתי ‘He said to them “What did I do ...” Then their anger against him softened when he spoke ...’ However, a YQTL form may also be used after אז in a past context, as
1 Kgs. 16:21 אז יחלק העם ישראל לחצי ‘At that time the people of Israel was divided in two.’ Rabinowitz has shown that the events represented by an imperfect form introduced by אז can be seen in all cases as having occurred during the general period of the events described in the preceding context, and in some cases must be seen so, as in this passage. (Rabinowitz [1984], pp. 54–56, but with a different understanding of the value of the verb form). That is, an imperfect introduced by אז represents an event which is present relative to its past context, just as with the uses of the imperfect form in a past context described as standard in ##8–10.The common opinion that imperfect forms following אז originated as preterites must contend with a variety of difficulties. Some are raised in Rabinowitz (1984), pp. 53–54. THE IDENTIFICATION OF MODAL FORMS
13. The modal system is represented by imperatives, used in affirm-
ative clauses with second person subject, and by the forms of the im-
perfect known as “jussive” and “cohortative” used where the clause is
negative, or where the subject is first or third person. Distinct modal
imperfect forms occur only where the subject is first person, 2m.s., or
3m./f.s. Any original difference between the modal and the indicative
forms of the imperfect has been lost where the subject is 2f.s., 2.pl, or
3.pl. (On forms with suffixes, see #14.3.) First person modal forms show
the affix ָה-; the corresponding imperfect forms do not. Forms from
roots IIIh show the “long” imperfect form (identical with the indicative
imperfect form) where a first person modal is expected. In 2m.s. and
3m./f.s. forms, where the imperfect form shows î or û in a final closed
syllable, the corresponding modal form shows e or o respectively. Where
the final syllable of the imperfect form is open, modal imperfect forms
from roots IIIh omit the final vowel. The same form from roots IIIy
is used in all situations. These forms from roots IIIy, first person forms
from roots IIIh, and all other forms which show no modal/indicative
distinction, are referred to here as “neutral” forms. First person modal
imperfect forms are called “affixed”. Second and third person forms
are called “short” in contrast to the “long” indicative forms. A form is
said to have “modal value” if used in a position in which the standard
system permits the use of modal forms but not indicative forms, as after
the negative אל. (12) Modal forms can be said to be used to present commands, requests, wishes, or
statements of firm intention, but a serious attempt to describe the function of modal forms

MODAL VERBS AND THE waw consecutive perfect
17. The material in #15–16, which lists the cases in which the use of imperfect forms marked as modal or indicative appears to be inconsistent with the conclusion reached in #14, provides no serious reason to doubt that conclusion. Consequently it can be stated that an imperfect form in the corpus, which begins its clause has modal value; an imperfect form which stands within its clause (and is not preceded by אל or followed by נא) has indicative value. Clearly, then, the waw consecutive perfect could only be a free variant of the modal imperfect, since it also begins its clause. It could, however, be a conditioned variant of the indicative imperfect; that is, it could have the grammatical function of representing a YQTL indicative verb in clause-initial position. That this would be a useful function is obvious. The main factor conditioning word order in biblical Hebrew is ‘thematization’.For the term ‘thematization,’ see Leech, 1981, p. 195. The importance of this factor is suggested by the traditional statement that an item was placed before the verb “for emphasis.” It is demonstrated in detail for constituents following the verb in Lode, 1984, and for verbless clauses in the corpus, with examples from verbal clauses, in Revell, 1989. The components of a clause are arranged in the order of their significance for the speaker or narrator. Modal verbs, which present commands, requests, etc. are typically the most significant component of their clause, and so stand first in it. However the significance of other verbs also often requires that they stand first in their clauses, particularly where sequences of events are depicted. Hence the need to distinguish modal from indicative verbs. The fact that the waw consecutive perfect is used to distinguish a clause-initial verb as a YQTL indicative is suggested by the following considerations.
17.1 In conditional sentences in which the apodosis begins with a waw consecutive perfect verb, the only function of the particle waw is to mark
22 E. J. REVELL [22]
the perfect form as ‘consecutive’. An apodosis which does not begin with a waw consecutive perfect is typically not introduced by a conjunction.An apodosis which follows the protasis is occasionally introduced by a conjunction, as in 1 Sam. 20:9, 2 Sam. 12:8, but this is exceptional. The contrast is well illustrated in the paired conditional sentences in Judg. 4:8, where one apodosis begins with והלכתי, the other with לא אלך, in sentences identical except for the negative. See also 1 Sam. 2:25. Where the apodosis precedes the protasis, an initial verb may have a prefixed conjunction which joins the sentence to what precedes, as in 2 Kgs. 18:23.
17.2 A waw consecutive perfect form follows an imperative in only about a quarter of the possible cases in the corpus, and follows a modal imperfect in little more than a tenth.This contrasts with the statement in Driver, 1892, #112, that the use of the perfect with waw consecutive “is by far the most common construction after an imperative.” Driver’s view is probably derived from the legal materials of the Pentateuch. This appears to be a second area in which the usage of the corpus differs significantly from that of these legal materials (see n. 7). In sharp contrast, clause initial verbs which carry on a sequence of indicatives are regularly waw consecutive in form. A waw consecutive perfect following a modal verb cannot, then, stand in the same sort of relationship to it as it does to a preceding indicative. Consequently it is reasonable to argue that the waw consecutive perfect represents the YQTL indicative as a conditioned variant of the imperfect, as suggested in #1. If this view is correct, a waw consecutive perfect following a modal verb must have connotations different from those of a modal verb in the same position. A survey of the use of the waw consecutive perfect suggests that this is indeed the case.
18. Where two imperatives are used in sequence, they often effectively represent a single command, which is expressed by the second of the two verbs, as where the first is a form of הלך ,קום, or שוב, with merely hortatory value. Thus in 1 Kgs. 19:7 קום אכל ‘Rise, eat’, the main point of the command is that Elijah should eat to gain strength for his journey. Even where the first of two imperatives is not merely hortatory, the second can often be understood as carrying the more significant component of the command. In contrast, a waw consecutive perfect used in sequence with an imperative typically represents an action to be taken as a consequence of carrying out the initial command represented by the imperative, as in 1 Sam. 9:19 ואכלתם... עלה ‘Go up ... and (then) you will eat’. The contrast can be illustrated from the use, in the corpus, of the forms of ישב and שוב following imperatives.
18.1 A form of ישב is the second of two imperatives in
1 Sam. 1:23 ... עשי הטוב בעיניך שבי ‘Do what you think best. Stay here

...’ The two commands require the same action, but this is described specifically only by the second.
2 Sam. 15:19 שוב ושב עם המלך ‘Go back and stay with the King.’ The significant part of the command — stay with the king where you will be secure — is carried by the second imperative.
2 Kgs. 14:10 הכבד ושב בביתך ‘Enjoy your honors and stay at home.’ Both verbs require the action specified by the second. In addition, this second verb is much the more significant of the two for the speaker, Jehoash, who wants to persuade Amaziah not to attack him.
A waw consecutive perfect form of ישב follows an imperative in

1 Kgs. 17:9 קום לך צרפתה ... וישבת שם Set out and go to Sarephath ... and stay there’. The significant command is to journey to Sarephath. The stay there will be an ensuing consequence.
18.2 An imperative of שוב represents the action actually required — ‘go back’ — after a hortatory imperative of הלך in 1 Kgs. 19:15, 20, 2 Kgs. 1:6. It also represents the more significant component of the command in 1 Sam. 15:30 ושוב עמי ... כבדני נא... ‘Do me honor ... come back with me’, and in 1 Kgs. 12:5 לכו עד שלשה ימים ושובו אלי ‘Come back after three days.’ A waw consecutive perfect form from שוב represents an action to be taken as a consequence of carrying out a command represented by a preceding imperative in: 1 Sam. 23:23 וראו ודעו ... ושבתם ... ‘Find out ... then return and tell me’; 2 Sam. 10:5 שבו ... ושבתם ‘Stay in Jericho until your beards are grown, then return’; 2 Sam. 11:15 הבו ... ושבתם ‘Put Uriah where the battle is fiercest, then withdraw’.
18.3 In these cases, then, a perfect with waw consecutive does seem to carry connotations different from those carried by an imperative, even though English usage typically requires that both be rendered as commands.
19. An imperative from one root may be followed by a verb from a second root which is imperative in form in some cases, perfect with waw consecutive in others. Where this occurs, the use of verb forms often cannot reasonably be explained by the argument in #18. Nevertheless, the two forms do seem to carry different connotations here as well. One

imperative is followed by another where the command is urgent, or is addressed to someone who is inferior in status, or is despised.Cf. the relation between the use of אל and לא in negative commands and the status of the person addressed suggested in Qimron, 1986, #400.13*. Where an imperative is followed by a perfect with waw consecutive, the situation is not urgent, and the command is given to someone who is esteemed. The examples from the corpus in which such use of forms from the same roots can be compared are:

An imperative form from אמר is used where the command is from a prophet to the wife of Jeroboam (1 Kgs. 14:7), to Obadiah (1 Kgs. 18:8, 11, 14), or to Hazael (2 Kgs. 8:10). Cf. 19.2 אכל . . . עלה (go up, eat). The imperative of אכל in 1 Kgs. 18:41 shows that the prophet despises Ahab, and/or that ‘eat’ is the main command; in 1 Sam. 9:19 the waw consecutive perfect shows that ‘go up’ is the main command (cf. #18).
19.3 The same phenomenon can be suggested where the second verb is jussive. Compare
1 Kgs. 22:6 עלה ויתן אדני ביד המלך ‘Go up. May the Lord give (it) to the King’ with
1 Kgs. 22:15 עלה והצלח ונתן יהוה ביד המלך ‘Go up and be successful. The Lord will give (it) to the King’ (cf. 1 Kgs. 22:12). In both cases the second verb, which carries on the modal sequence, gives encouragement for success. In the second example a confirming statement is added with a waw consecutive perfect. Another example with a jussive form is discussed in #24.1.
19.4 A final example with an imperative can be offered where different roots are used, but the actions they represent are similar. In 1 Kgs. 22:26 the imperatives קח את מיכיהו והשיבהו . . . present a command delivered by the King to unnamed officials. The main component of the command is carried by the second verb ‘Take Mikayah and return him . . . to the city governor (to prison)’. In 1 Kgs. 1:33 קחו . . . והרכבתם . . . present a request by David to his senior officials to ‘Take with you your masters’ servants, and place my son on a mule (to be annointed as heir designate)’.

19.5 The waw consecutive perfect is translated as an imperative in accordance with English usage in this case, as in the others, but the use of this form shows that the verb is a YQTL indicative, with connotations different from those carried by an imperative or other modal form. A modal form is used to present a forceful command, whether its force reflects the fact that, although not first in a series of commands, it is of major significance, or reflects the urgency of the situation, or the social or moral status of the speaker relative to the person addressed. The waw consecutive perfect (a YQTL indicative form) is used in the same context to present a command which is less forceful, whether the (relative) lack of force reflects the fact that the action to be taken is a later consequence of action already forcefully commanded, or that it is not urgent, or that there is no wish to mark any difference of social or moral status between the speaker and the person addressed. It must be admitted (with Joüon, 1947, 301) that the different values of the waw consecutive perfect and imperative following an imperative are not always significant in the contexts in which they are used. Similarly, in English, the four possible variations of ‘I sang/was singing as I walked/was walking’ could be used in the same context with no significant difference of connotation. That does not mean, however, that the two past forms have the same meaning. So also the simple equation “after an imperative, waw consecutive perfect = imperative” is an oversimplification; it hides the function of the waw consecutive perfect as presenting a clause-initial indicative, with its particular connotations. Just as with QTL and YQTL forms, which are typically used in different contexts as having distinct values, and which present different connotations in those contexts in which either can be used, so with the two forms with present/future value: modal and YQTL indicative. In a context established as one in which directions are given by a preceding imperative (or otherwise as 2 Sam. 14:10, 1 Kgs. 13:31, quoted in #20.2), either an indicative or an imperative form can be used, and the connotations they present are different.
20.1 Where the verb does not begin the clause, the YQTL category must be represented by an imperfect form. This is used after an imperative with the same connotations as a clause-initial waw consecutive perfect; that is, it presents a continuation of the command in a less forceful register. Examples of imperfect forms used in this way are:
Judg. 6:25 קח את פר השור . . . והרסת את מזבח הבעל . . . ואת האשרה אשר עליו תכרת ‘Take the bullock . . . Then you must tear down the Baal altar . . . and cut down the Asherah which is beside it.’

The essential syntax in this last example is the same as that of
1 Sam. 10:2 בלכתך היום מעמדי ומצאת ‘When you leave me today, you will meet . . .’ The fact that English would use a command or request in the first example, but a statement in the second, is indicated by the content of the words and their context. It is not indicated either by their forms or by their syntax. That is, Hebrew and English use of imperative (jussive) and indicative is not the same. The conventions of English (or other European languages) must, of course, be respected in translation, but cannot be used to determine the significance of the Hebrew forms. This point may be emphasized by a final example
Judg. 6:17 ... אם נא מצאתי חן בעיניך ועשית לי אות ‘If (please) I have found favor in your sight (you will) give me a sign . . .’ English would typically translate the waw consecutive perfect by an imperative. However an imperative form would be perfectly acceptable in that position in Hebrew. Consequently it seems highly probable that the use of the waw consecutive perfect in the apodosis, rather than an imperative, signals humility

21. As is well known, לא with the imperfect is used in early materials to present a particularly forceful prohibition.This usage does not seem to be current in the corpus. אל and לא appear equivalent in 1 Kgs. 20:8 אל תשמע ולוא תאבה ‘Do not listen and do not agree.’ Similarly in 2 Sam. 5:23 לא תעלה ‘do not go up (to attack)’ is not a particularly forceful command. A modal verb is not used in the same context in יהוה יעלה ‘Judah will go up’ (Judg. 1:2). The negatives אל and לא appear to vary freely in prohibitions at Qumran. (See Qimron, 1986:400.13*) However it is obvious that, both in early materials and in the corpus, לא with an imperfect can present a statement, as well as a command. In
2 Sam. 21:17 לא תצא ... ולא תכבה ‘Do not go out to battle with us any more, and you will not quench the lamp of Israel’. The translation of one verb as a command and the other as a statement is a matter of English usage, reflecting an understanding of the content of the clauses and their context. There is nothing in the form of the verbs or their syntax which requires translation in either way. Similar usage is found in Akkadian, where la taparras can present either a command or a prediction. The same is true of ‘you will not do’ in English. In the latter case, the two values are distinguished by intonation patterns, as well as by the context in which they are used. In written texts, only the latter criterion is available. As for the relative forcefulness of the indicative and imperative patterns, this depends on the conventions of the users. My own impression is that in English, as in Hebrew, the statement ‘You will not do’ typically presents a more forceful prohibition than the imperative ‘do not’, whereas the imperative ‘do’ presents a more urgent command than the statement ‘you will do’.

HISTORICAL CONSIDERATIONS
23. The above survey shows that a plausible case can be made in support of the contention that waw consecutive perfect forms represent clause-initial YQTL verbs, and that indicative verbs carry a meaning distinct from that of modals. That this case is valid, and not merely plausible, can be argued from the changes which occurred in the verb system of later Biblical Hebrew, as shown in the books of Daniel, Ezra, and Nehemiah. The use of verbs in these books can be briefly described as follows.
23.1 The use of QTL forms does not differ significantly from that of standard prose, but there is a morphological innovation. First person imperfect forms with waw consecutive commonly show affixed ־ה. This is a late usage which became standard in the Hebrew of Qumran (see Qimron, 1986, #310.122, and Revell, 1988).
30 E. J. REVELL [30]
23.2 Imperfect forms in clause-initial position are regularly short, affixed, or neutral; those used within clauses are regularly long or neutral. However this formal contrast does not mark any semantic difference, as is shown by the fact that second person imperfect forms may begin clauses (Dan. 9:25, 12:13, also Neh. 9:28 in a past context).There are some exceptions. Affixed first person forms fail to occur where expected in Neh. 2:18, 5:12, 6:10, 10:32 (cf. #15.1). A long 3rd person imperfect form begins a clause which is closely related to the preceding in Dan. 12:12 אשרי המחכה ויגיע ‘Blessed be he who waits and reaches . . .’; also Dan. 12:4; and, in a past context, Neh. 3:14. Presumably the close semantic relationship (possibly reflected in intonation contours) shows that the verb is indicative (see #15.3, 4). The same usage may account for the long qere form in Dan. 11:10 ישוב ויתגרה ‘He will return and wage war’. A long clause-initial imperfect occurs where no such relationship obtains in Dan. 12:13 (2m.s.) and Neh. 3:15 (qere, 3m.s., with past value). A short imperfect form occurs within a clause in Dan. 9:16 (before נא), Ezra 1:3 (after an extraposed constituent), and in Neh. 3:37, 13:14, after the negative אל where it begins the clause. However a long form is used after אל in Neh. 3:37 where it does not begin the clause.
23.3 The use of imperative forms follows the standard pattern, including that of the sequence of modals (#14.4). One imperative follows another in 22 cases. An imperative follows a jussive (marked by following נא) in Neh. 1:11. A jussive (marked by אל) follows an imperative in Neh. 3:37, as does a neutral imperfect in Dan. 1:12. The perfect with waw consecutive is not used in sequence with imperatives.
23.4 (Apart from use after imperatives) the waw consecutive perfect and the imperfect with conjunctive waw are free variants in clause initial position, as can be seen from the mixture of forms in sequence in Dan. 11:5, 7, 10, 15, etc.This also occurs in materials from Qumran, as in 1QS 4:20–21 . . . ואז יברר . . . וזק . . . חק; but the waw consecutive perfect seems usually to be used to represent a clause initial future indicative at Qumran, as in the standard usage of the corpus.

It could be argued that the anomalies listed in #16.3, 4, show that the language of the corpus was already close to this situation, and that the different connotations ascribed to modal and indicative forms in many other cases are illusory. Thus שוב עמי ואשתחוה (with an imperfect in modal position 1 Sam. 15:25) and שוב עמי והשתחויתי (with a YQTL indicative, 1 Sam. 15:30) could carry exactly the same message ‘Return with me and I will worship’ (although they could show a shift from modal to indicative to express greater politeness/humility; see #20, especially Judg. 6:17 in #20:2). However the fact that different grammatical categories may, in some cases, be used without distinction does not show that they are never distinct. The difference of implication exists potentially in all cases, even though it may not be significant in all.
It has been shown above that the semantic fields of the two indicative categories overlap in a number of cases, so that either can be used to represent an action where such overlap occurs. The categories are, however, distinct in meaning; each carries connotations different from the other. Consequently, the possibility of choosing either category in such a situation allows the narrator to extend his range of expression beyond the limitations of morphology, and present a range of temporal or aspectual nuances comparable to that achieved in Indo-European languages through the greater variety of forms. The use of YQTL forms in sequence with modals, or in other situations in which they appear to present commands, etc. is an example of the same phenomenon. The fact that modal and indicative forms are occasionally used in the corpus without appreciable difference in meaning may reflect the beginning of the development which led to the complete loss of distinction between them, but not more than the beginning. The indicative and modal categories in the corpus are no less distinct in meaning than are the QTL and YQTL categories.
24.2 The distinction of the modal or indicative value of neutral imperfect forms by their position in the clause must have been a firmly fixed feature of the language, since it still governs the position in which short and affixed imperfect forms, or long imperfect forms, are used in Daniel, Ezra, and Nehemiah, even though the forms do not differ in meaning. The use of verbs in these three books also differs from that standard in the corpus in some other respects. The waw consecutive perfect is not used after imperatives. Elsewhere, it is a free variant of clause-initial imperfects, and so has no special function. Second person
imperfects are used in clause-initial position, and an indicative imperfect form may be used where an imperfect is medial in a semantic unit, even where it is initial in a clause. These features suggest a considerable development from the pattern standard in the corpus towards the usage characteristic of Mishnaic Hebrew. It seems clear that a major cause of this development was the loss of distinction between the modal and indicative values of the imperfect.
THE SYSTEM OF THE VERB IN STANDARD BIBLICAL PROSE
25. A verb can be marked as modal in the corpus by its form (imperative, or short or affixed imperfect), by its position (initial in its clause) or by co-occurrence (with following נא or preceding אל). Any one of these marks will serve to identify it, but it may have two, or even three of them. A YQTL indicative is marked by a waw consecutive perfect form in clause-initial position, or by an imperfect form (not in co-occurrence with נא or אל) within a clause.
25.1 It is possible that the different modal forms in Hebrew are vestiges of more complete “imperative”, and “short”, and “affixed” imperfect paradigms, each of which had a distinct function. In standard Hebrew prose, however, they form a single set of modal forms, and in many cases the same “neutral” imperfect form is used for both modal and indicative functions. Due to the relation between the significance of a constituent and its position in the clause (see #17), verbs with modal value typically stood in clause-initial position. Consequently indicative imperfect forms came to be restricted to position within the clause, so that the value of a neutral imperfect was marked as modal if it began the clause, as indicative if it did not (unless it was marked as modal by a particle). The waw consecutive perfect (the origin of which is not known) came to be used where a YQTL indicative verb was required in clause-initial position, and so as a positional variant of the indicative imperfect. While this pattern continued to govern the positions in which the modal and indicative forms of the imperfect were used, the difference in their values was lost, so that the imperative eventually became the only distinct modal form, as in Mishanic Hebrew. This development may be foreshadowed in the partial blurring of the distinction between the values of modal and indicative forms in the corpus. It was possibly influenced, in its later stages, by the vernacular language. The development resulted in the abandonment of the features which had distinguished modal imperfects from YQTL indicatives, including the use of the waw consecutive perfect, because it took away their function. This
process is quite advanced in the language of Qumran (see Qimron, 1986, #400.03*; Kutscher, 1974:357–8).
26. A QTL indicative is represented in the corpus by a perfect form within a clause, or at the beginning of a clause where the conjunction waw is not used. Where the conjunction is used, the QTL indicative is typically represented by the waw consecutive imperfect. This form derives from the original “preterite”, which early became restricted, in prose, to initial position in a clause which was part of a sequence, or was presented as such, and so began with a conjunction. Here it acts as a positional variant of the perfect, and functions to indicate the structure of narrative passages. The perfect form with a prefixed conjunction represents QTL in a past context in a number of cases in which the action is considered as identical with, or as a facet of, that of the preceding clause. This is distinct from the waw consecutive use of the perfect (which is restricted to a present/future context) and is common enough in the corpus that it can be regarded as a feature of standard usage. It is possible that, in an earlier phase, the waw consecutive imperfect was the only representative of QTL used in clause-initial position with a prefixed conjunction, and that this use of the perfect was the first symptom of the change which eventually led to the complete replacement of the waw consecutive imperfect by the perfect. However this may be, the waw consecutive imperfect appears to have been used according to the standard pattern throughout the biblical period and also in the literary language of Qumran. In 1QIsaa its replacement by the perfect is rare in comparison to the number of cases in which the waw consecutive perfect is replaced by the imperfect (see Kutscher, 1974:354–5, 357–8).
27. The use of verbs in the corpus is, then, a complex, but generally consistent system representing a more or less stable stage of usage characteristic of the prose narrative of a particular period. Since it is a stage in continuing development, it is not surprising that the usage is not entirely consistent. Possibly some of the unusual features found in it are vestiges of the usage of earlier stages, restricted, like English subjunctives, to particular contexts. Others may well be early examples of usage which became standard in the succeeding stage. No doubt some of the anomalies it shows arose from errors in transmission. The standard pattern of the usage is, however, clear. The most interesting feature brought out by this survey is the grammatical function of the waw consecutive perfect, which marks a clause initial verb as a YQTL indicative.
